chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 171 to 180, Ammuvanar's Thondi decade, a linked chain in which each poem opens with the last words of the one before and every poem likens the girl to the Chera port of Thondi: by our reading the man, struck by her, loses his heart and his sleep, is granted a tryst, pleads with her and her friend, and then the friend turns his own word, grace, back on him and asks for marriage.

171.reading: The man says the young woman with bright bangles and shoulders full as bamboo, lovely as Thondi where the sweet sound of the waves mingles with the sweet sound of drums beaten along every street, has carried off his heart.
171.nuance: The town is heard before it is seen: the sea's music and the drums of the streets blend into one sound, and that is what the girl is likened to. The last words, the girl who took my heart, are taken up as the first words of 172, beginning the decade's linked chain.

thinai_evidence.note: the sound of the sea's waves in a shore town

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders, and through them the girl

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man speaks of the girl in the first person (என், எமக்கு) during the secret love, and the decade's linked chain carries his voice from poem to poem; the addressee, his companion, is a guess

172.reading: The man says the bright-bangled girl has taken his heart, and like the waves of the strong sea that roar at the bee-loud cool ford of Thondi, he does not know sleep even at night.
172.nuance: The sea is chosen because it never rests: what is a pleasant background roar in 171 has become, one poem later, the measure of a man who cannot lie still.

thinai_evidence.note: the cold ford and the sea at night

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man speaks of the girl in the first person (என், எமக்கு) during the secret love, and the decade's linked chain carries his voice from poem to poem; the addressee, his companion, is a guess

173.reading: Those seized by the dark braided hair that smells of the cool fragrant neythal flowers of Thondi, the man says, do not know sweet sleep even at night and suffer a cutting pain.
173.nuance: He speaks of himself in the third person plural, as if stating a law: whoever is struck by such hair suffers so. The hair is named as the அணங்கு, the afflicting power, so the girl is a danger as well as a beauty. அரவுறு துயரம் may be the pain of a file's cut or of a snake's bite; either way a bodily wound.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal flower of the backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man speaks of the girl in the first person (என், எமக்கு) during the secret love, and the decade's linked chain carries his voice from poem to poem; the general plural (அணங்குற்றோர், those seized) reads as the man answering a companion who blames him

174.reading: The man says the girl of fine jewels, with collyrium eyes where red veins spread and a lovely glowing body, has granted him in his weariness a tryst in a fragrant grove like Thondi of the cool, goddess-haunted ford.
174.nuance: The haunted ford answers the அணங்கு of 173: the power that struck him now grants him a meeting. Line 4 is hard: அம் கலிழ் மேனி may be her glowing body or a body clouded with tears, and அசைஇய may describe him as worn out or her as at rest.

thinai_evidence.note: the cold ford and the shore grove of the tryst

comparisons.tenor: the fragrant grove of the tryst, or the girl who grants it

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man speaks of the girl in the first person (என், எமக்கு) during the secret love, and the decade's linked chain carries his voice from poem to poem

175.reading: The man asks the young woman, if she has love and pity for him, to come walking slowly with her friend of the bamboo shoulders and bright brow, bringing with her the many qualities that make her like Thondi.
175.nuance: Asking her to come with her friend, slowly, is asking for a meeting that looks like an ordinary walk. Line 4 பண்புல is read as பண்பு பல, the many qualities; 176 opens with பண்பும, which supports the word பண்பு.

thinai_evidence.note: no native thing beyond the town's name; the colophon's neythal is accepted

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the vocative மடந்தை and the plea to come (வந்திசின்) make the man the speaker and the girl the addressee

176.reading: The man asks the friend to tell the bright-bangled girl her fault: she, fragrant with the cool new flowers of Thondi, with finely made wide hips and a body like plucked tender shoots, has taken away both his good nature and his bed.
176.nuance: The charge is theft: பண்பும் பாயலும் கொண்டனள், she has taken my nature and my bed, so the lover frames his sleeplessness as a wrong done to him that the friend must name to her.

thinai_evidence.note: the new flowers of the shore town

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; கூறுமதி (please tell) asks a third person to speak, read as the man pleading with the girl's friend

177.reading: Those who have touched the shoulders of the woman like Thondi, the man says, where the fragrant sea-holly flowers scent the long ridge of heaped sand on which the greedy waves play, will surely tremble even if they have done no wrong.
177.nuance: The trembling is not guilt, the poem insists, so it can only be the woman's power working on whoever has embraced her; the waves that endlessly play on the sand give that restlessness a shore.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea holly on the dune of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man speaks of the girl in the first person (என், எமக்கு) during the secret love, and the decade's linked chain carries his voice from poem to poem; தவறிலர் ஆயினும் (even if they did no wrong) reads as an answer to a companion who blames him

178.reading: The man asks whether he can live merely by praising her shoulders and hair again and again, if she, who is like Thondi of Kuttuvan of the just sceptre, sees him and still does not love him and grant him grace.
178.nuance: The just sceptre is not idle praise of the king: a town under a just ruler gives to all who come, and the lover who calls her such a town is asking for that same grace. Praise alone, he says, cannot keep him alive.

thinai_evidence.note: no native thing beyond the shore town's name; the colophon's neythal is accepted

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; நீ நல்காக் கால் (if you do not grant grace) addresses the girl directly

179.reading: The friend asks the lord of the shore of dense waters to be gracious, for the small brow of this girl, who has no one but him, is like sweet-sounding Thondi, where prawns leap at the ford when the crab strikes.
179.nuance: The voice turns here from the man to the friend, and his own word நல்கு from 178 comes back at him as her demand. A near miss for ullurai: the crab's strike and the prawn's leap could stand for the man and the startled girl, but the poem gives no anchor for a second pair, so they are scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the crab of the ford and the lord of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the vocative சேர்ப்ப and இவள் (this girl) make the friend the speaker, pleading for the heroine

180.reading: The friend tells the man to marry her and then take this small bud, her beauty, which is like Thondi of the ford where the old heron that can no longer fly lives on the rich fish the netters of the great waters bring.
180.nuance: The heron that can no longer fly yet is fed by the netters is not tagged as iraicchi, since it acts only by being fed; but it sits beside a girl said in 179 to have no one but him, and a reader may hear in it the dependent who must be provided for. The order matters: வரைந்தனை கொண்மோ, marry first, then take her.

thinai_evidence.note: the heron and the fishermen of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; வரைந்தனை கொண்மோ (marry, then take) is the friend's call for marriage, continuing 179

links.note: Both set a wing-worn heron at the ford of Thondi: Kuruntokai 128's பறைதபு நாரை on the eastern sea longs in vain for the ayirai fish of Thondi's harbour, as the man's heart longs for a distant girl; Ainkurunuru 180's பறைதபு முதுகுருகு sits fed on the rich fish the netters bring.
links.teaches: The flightless heron of Thondi is hopeless longing when it must reach the fish itself and secure dependence when the fishermen bring the fish to it, so the friend's version answers the lover's lament: the helpless are fed only when someone provides, which is what she asks the man to do by marrying.

links.note: Both liken the girl to Kuttuvan's Thondi: in Ainkurunuru 178 the courting man calls her like Thondi of Kuttuvan of the just sceptre, while in Akananuru 290 the heroine says her eyes, once like the neythal of Kuttuvan's Thondi harbour, have lost that likeness and turned pale while he delays marriage.
links.teaches: The Thondi likeness is the lover's praise in courtship and becomes the heroine's own measure of loss when marriage is delayed, so the beauty the man praises to win her is the very thing his delay spends, and the friend of 179 and 180 is right to press him.

links.note: Both have the man name the girl's power with the word அணங்கு: in Kural 1081 he cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; in Ainkurunuru 173 her fragrant hair is the அணங்கு and those it seizes lose their sleep.
links.teaches: The Kural leaves the smitten man's question open, and the Sangam poem answers it not by settling what she is but by the symptom, sleepless nights and a cutting pain, so that in the tradition the afflicting goddess is known by what she does to the one who sees her.

links.note: Both have the man in secret love say the girl keeps his eyes from sleep at night: Ainkurunuru 172 likens his wakefulness to the never-resting waves of Thondi; Kural 1136 has him, sleepless at midnight, think of riding the palmyra horse.
links.teaches: Ainkurunuru 172 stops at the sleepless night and gives it the image of the restless sea, while the Kural shows where that night leads, to the threat of the madal, so the pair marks sleeplessness as the stage of love just before shame is given up.

source_issues: Every colophon of the decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speakers and addressees are inferred from the poems and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
175 line 4 பண்புல gives no clear word; read as பண்பு பல (many qualities), uncertain.
174 line 4 அம் கலிழ் மேனி அசைஇய எமக்கே is hard to construe: கலிழ் may be glowing or weeping, and அசைஇய may refer to the man's weariness or the girl's rest.
173 line 2 அரவுறு may be from அரம் (a file) or அரவு (a snake); the sense of pain is clear, the image is not.
The decade is a linked chain (each poem opens with the last words of the one before) except at 180, which opens with சிறுநனை after 179 ends with சிறு நுதலே, taking up only சிறு.
